I was active, I was a strong man, able-bodied, and that's why he took me to work for him. It's not what I wanted. And they kept these signatures. If anything went wrong, they wanted to show it in court or somewhere, that I voluntarily took up their arms to voluntarily join their paramilitary unit allegedly to protect my family or something. I think it is in my statement. I said that at the outset. Those who stayed loyal to them, they kind of protected them because they had killed everyone else. Everyone that remained alive were put in work platoons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for the witness, of course. Witness, at the end of the war, did the commander of the unit in which you worked in the labour platoon, did this person propose -- did the people who made you sign this statement that the Prosecutor just mentioned, did these people, the commander or the authorities, did they ask you whether you wanted to move to the territory of Republika Srpska or even move to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They used to tell me, this commander, Rajko Jankovic, and others to accept, to be loyal to them, in order to be able to stay with my family like they did. They told me, "Whether you accept or not, you can't return to Sarajevo to be with your own people. Either you're going to get killed here or we are going to kill you." That was the only choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question on this issue, and then I'll move to my final point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In this conflict, what was your objective? Was it to fight against the Muslims, was it to survive with your family, was it to become a hero? What was your objective?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was on my mind. I just wanted my family to survive and for myself to survive. Had they told me to do anything, I would have had to do it when they demanded that. They always made threats vis a vis my family, saying that they would slaughter my son and daughter, rape my wife, so I'd have to agree to anything they'd tell me to do, because I could not watch with my very own eyes what they would do to my wife and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I will now move to my final point. The visit made by Mr. Seselj to the Crna Rijeka Plateau, a visit which you have mentioned, could you tell us how long -- how long did the combat go on at that plateau? Was it for a couple days, a couple months? Can you tell us how long they went on for?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Crna Rijeka Plateau, when the offensive just started there, for two or three hours they were attacking that village. When they took the village, they went further on to the village of Olovo. Along the frontline, they went to the village of Olovo; that is to say, that they'd be there for months. That is where the frontline was, and they maintained it that way. While this line was being attacked, it was something that went on for three or four hours, this offensive. They did whatever they wanted to. That's the way it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether, when you made written statements to the local authorities and whether in your first statements made to the OTP and to the Tribunal investigators, could you tell us whether you were questioned about Mr. Seselj or not, whether there was focus on Mr. Seselj, "yes" or "no," during these early statements that you made?

utterances.speaker: SAFET SEJDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they didn't ask me about Mr. Seselj then. I made my statement here, and I said what I said. When I came here, I didn't know what the objective was, who I would testify against. Just before I was about to leave, I was told that I would be testifying against Mr. Seselj. I remembered then that I saw him at the Crna Rijeka Plateau, and I said that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no other questions, Mr. President. However, I have some information to give you, if you find it useful, for the two MFI exhibits that I was going to tender -- try to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first document was a list of houses in Svrake, empty and unoccupied houses. It's document P463, MFI. This document is part of what we call the integration collection. Those are documents collected by AID in the Sarajevo sector, after having been handed over in 1996 by the authorities of Republika Srpska. According to AID, this document would have been received from the General Staff, Army Security Service -- Security Service of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the OTP members collected -- went to the AID premises to get these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor is not resolving the problem of the authenticity of the document in this way at all. The re-examination is over, and this is now a procedural debate on the acceptability or non-acceptability of some documents. I challenge the documents because there is no signature, stamp, letterhead, nothing. And now, as an argument to prove authenticity, the Prosecutor refers to the AID. Well, that is the core of the matter. The AID instrumentalizes witnesses who appear in The Hague Tribunal in different trials. They falsify documents and so on. They are very involved in this. They cannot be proof of authenticity. The document either has a signature or not, it either has a stamp or not, it either has a registration number or not. If we are going to refer to AID, then you can immediately find evidence for anything you want to prove here. In 15 minutes' time, the AID will type that up, write it up. They can even make the documents look older.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's as far as the first document goes. The second document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted very candidly to give the background regarding this evidence. I cannot be reproached for that, knowing that the witness gave us some explanation of the document tells who were the -- which were the people who were in the premises, and so on and so forth. So now it's a matter of weight, as far as I go. Now, regarding the second document, considering the list of prisoners, P464 MFI, this document was seized by the OTP in July 2003 in the archives of the prison KPD Butmir, or better known as the Kula Prison, and more precisely this document was seized out of a green folder called Daily Bulletin of the Vogosca Prison for July and August 1992. So, Prison of Vogosca, July and August of 1992. And you'll remember that at the very end of this document, they were making reference to other documents. You put -- you were wondering whether we had it or not. The only document that I was able to find so far was a document that regards a list of prisoners. They have it in e-court. I have hard copies, if you wish to get them. Now, as far as the other documents, I don't know if they were -- as far as the others, I don't know if they were missing in the prison or other people collected these documents. I have no additional information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, on the second document, do you have any comments to make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I haven't seen that document yet in e-court. I have to see what this is all about. Secondly, let the OTP tell me whether I've already received this document and when, because I cannot remember all the documents that I've received. I've already received hundreds of thousands of pages of documents. And then when the Prosecution replies to that question of mine, then I'm going to put forth my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This document, when was it given to Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the exhibit list I don't know when. Probably pursuant to 66(B). But, anyhow, this document is on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This document was on the 65 ter list documents. Mr. Seselj, do you have any points? Do you challenge anything about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Taking prisoners out to the frontline, exposing them to risks, and we see here that one person was wounded, that is a crime, and I do not challenge the fact that it is a crime. However, there is no proof of this document being authentic. There is no signature, there is no stamp, there is no registration number. And what I think of straight away is the AID wrote this up themselves. They had an original document as a template, so to speak, and then they just changed a few words, and that is always my suspicion as far as these documents are concerned. Secondly, there is also the question of relevancy, because the prison warden is under the Ministry of Justice. The OTP takes a statement from the then Minister of Justice, submits it to me. They haven't called him as a witness yet. What do I have to do with that Minister of Justice, and what do I have to do with the system of prisoners? So it's the question of relevancy. If the then Minister of Justice is not held accountable for this but if they plan to use his statement against me in any way, I think from the point of procedure, this is practically an unresolvable problem. Secondly, perhaps all of this is correct, but then it raises the question of the responsibility of the person who took the prisoners out to the frontline to do work. That is prohibited by the International Law of War. It is not prohibited to take members of the work platoon to work on the frontline, because they are within the system of national defence. Taking prisoners out, that is a crime punishable by law. Who is this being ascribed to? Myself, personally, the Serb Radical Party, our volunteers? Who? Who is being charged with this crime, if this crime ever took place? First of all, what happened, and secondly, who is responsible? Who is immediately responsible, who is responsible at the next degree of responsibility from the point of view of hierarchy, and last but not least, thirdly, what does this have to do with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your comments are noted in the transcript. The Trial Chamber will deliberate on it and will render a decision. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 42, line 7, one point. I mention the transcript page, but there is a mistake. I mention page 8239, page 42, line 7, and not 72. Page 42, line 7, we should read page of the transcript -- transcript pages 8249.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this correction. On my name and on behalf of my fellow Judges, I thank you very much for coming to testify before this Tribunal. I wish you a safe journey back home, and I will ask Madam Usher to escort you out of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In advance, thank you very much to all of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still one problem. It's not 8249 but 8239 on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's now move into private session. The next witness has protective measures. Madam Registrar, actually, I would like to ask you for a closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the blinds are going down, have you admitted this document into evidence or not? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both documents are going to be the subject of a deliberation. They are not admitted yet. We have to deliberate on this, and we will render a decision. They are not admitted into evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
